newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hang Seng well placed to face competition.
newsitem.headline: Hang Seng well placed to face competition.

text.p: Hang Seng Bank Ltd said on Monday it is well placed to face the keen competition expected in Hong Kong's banking industry this year.
"Hang Seng is particularly well placed to face the competition," vice-chairman and chief executive Alex Au told a news conference.
Intense competition was expected to remain in the sector even though an anticipated improvement in the local economy would benefit the industry, he said.
Au said he expected growth in the bank's trade finance business this year on an expected improvement in the territory's trade. But he gave no projected figures.
Its trade finance advances stood at HK$15.73 billion last year, down from HK$15.93 billion in 1995.
Au said he also expected a smaller net provision for bad and doubtful debts this year than in 1996, when the net charge for such debts hit HK$715 million, a rise of HK$584 million on 1995.
"We are confident about out loan quality," he said. "I don't see a continuation of the provisioning level as...in 1996. We'll see a significant improvement in that area."
He attributed the rise in its 1996 net provision mainly to provisions made for "a few trade finance and corporate exposures", and said the 1996 provision level was still "comfortable".

Au agreed the interest margin for residential mortgage loans might be narrowed this year in the face of competition, and admitted such competition last year had an impact on the bank's market share in the mortgage loans in 1996.
But he did not give figures on market share.
Residential mortgage loans grew to HK$57.28 billion last year from HK$50.72 billion in 1995. Last year, such loans accounted for about 35 percent of the bank's total loans.
The bank could improve its interest margin by raising its loans-to-deposits ratio which is known to be low, he said.
The ratio of advances (including trade bills) to deposits rose to 51.2 percent as at the end of 1996 compared with 49.0 percent a year earlier.

Au attributed the widening in the bank's 1996 net interest margin, which rose 30 basis points to 3.10 percent per annum, to a loan growth of 16 percent, small growth in deposit interest rates, and better capital management.
